sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Kimi K3.1 Pro fourth on the independent index, the LiteLLM and eMudhra trust failures, DeepSeek's open engine, native PyTorch on TPU and Trainium, and public red-teams of agent monitors. Holds the score against cost chart.
sections.lead: Five stories. Two are about infrastructure being opened: DeepSeek's production engine and PyTorch on non-NVIDIA chips. Two are about trust failing or being tested: a signed pipeline that shipped malware, a CA whose keys could be computed, and monitors that miss most determined attacks. The fifth is the model of the week, which is mostly a lesson in reading scores with their harnesses.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: Open-weight follow-ups (MiniMax M3.1 Flash and Beam out, Mistral Large 4 still pending), Mercury 3, Mistral's speech and time-series models, small local and speech models, more decision models; no frontier-lab model.
sections.lead: A quiet week for the five largest labs and a busy one for weights promised earlier: two of the three open releases owed by last issue arrived, one with a licence that charges large commercial users. The new models are mostly specialists: speech, time series, decision and local coding models, each with vendor numbers and few independent ones yet.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: GRAFT and the scaffold-separation proof (both now paper pages), harness-gap follow-ups, what RL adds, reward hacking, distillation, synthetic data, speculative decoding, low-bit training and agent safety. Holds the GRAFT before/after animation.
sections.lead: The research thread of the week is measurement done properly: what RL changes token by token, what a harness adds that distillation cannot, how much drafter gains survive a fair baseline, and where a monitor should act in training. Most items are single-lab preprints; the cards say which numbers are the authors' own.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: OpenAI's reported round and Anthropic's draft S-1, Meta's capex, the DHS order on DeepSeek, GPT-6 on all three clouds, funding and policy reports.
sections.lead: Most big-tech earnings land just after this window, so the money news is reported rather than filed: a round, a draft prospectus and one quarter (Meta's). The durable items are distribution (every frontier lab now sells through every large cloud) and a US order whose reach extends to products built on open weights.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: Rubin's first cloud customer, NVIDIA's GTC Berlin, Cerebras across 59 wafers, HBM estimates, power as the binding constraint, rental readings.
sections.lead: Vera Rubin finally reached a customer, though not general availability, and the rest of the tab is about what limits deployment: wafers' SRAM capacity, HBM4 supply, and above all grid power, which is now cancelling deals and deciding sites.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: Claude API 2026-10-21 drops sampling parameters, Claude Duet, four standards into the Agentic AI Foundation, coding-agent and serving releases, caching and durability, DuckDB 2.0, TypeScript and JAX.
sections.lead: An API version that removes knobs, a foundation that collects agent standards, and release notes across the stack. The practical thread is that agents are now infrastructure: they get durable logs, cache breakpoints, safety telemetry and their own governance.

sections.name: Security
sections.label: Security
sections.glance: PHP2Shell, a Brotli RCE across runtimes, credential brokering for agents, Claude reducing attack surface, and a vendor study of persona-dependent code security.
sections.lead: The week's security news beyond the top story: two widely deployed native-code flaws found partly by AI tools, and the pattern that answers the LiteLLM incident, agents that use credentials without ever holding them.

sections.name: Talk of the town

sections.glance: The week's most-argued threads: no AI payoff outside tech, why labs do not start companies, shipping code you do not understand, price cuts, and why AI prose is hard to read.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: One week, 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-26: 70 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools, security and the week's arguments, each with its sources. The issue was written from the sources on 2026-10-26; where a claim rests on one outlet or a vendor, its card says so. This tab is the week in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The week's theme: the plumbing everyone trusts was opened up, attacked or audited. DeepSeek published the engine behind its service and PyTorch went native on TPU and Trainium, so two pieces of infrastructure that were private or awkward are now open. At the same time a signed release pipeline shipped malware, a certificate authority's keys turned out to be computable, and two public red-teams found that the monitors watching coding agents miss more than half of determined attacks. The model news fits the pattern: Kimi K3.1 Pro brings an open-weight-to-be model within three points of the top of the independent index, and its Terminal-Bench score depends on whose harness ran it. The [[score against cost chart|t-top|v-cost]] places K3.1 Pro, and the [[GRAFT animation|t-research|v-graft]] shows a different way to use a monitor in training.

1.short: Kimi K3.1 Pro: 4th on the index
notes: Checked 2026-10-26 against Moonshot's post and Artificial Analysis's launch article and model page: 55 on Intelligence Index v4.3.2, 2.8T / 104B active (Artificial Analysis), $1.98 per index task; Vals AI Terminal-Bench 4.0 and Vals Index figures read the same day. No K3.1 repository was on Hugging Face on 26 October.
The [[score against cost chart|t-top|v-cost]] below places K3.1 Pro against the models of the last two issues.

Checked 2026-10-26: the affected artefacts, times and the clean version (1.106.2) against LiteLLM's two posts; the payload against SafeDep's analysis. LiteLLM's first post said Claude Code may put a user's GitHub CLI token into response bodies that reach gateway logs; its later attack-chain post says the first token came from a different service.

Hacker News: eMudhra's disclosure 1,281 points and 504 comments, its exit from TLS 1,155 and 748; Railway's disclosure 602 and 341 (read 2026-10-26). PHP2Shell, the week's third infrastructure story, is in [[Security|t-sec|i-php2shell]].

Checked 2026-10-26 against the repository README (read through raw.githubusercontent.com): scope, hardware, parallel layout, DSpark, batch invariance and the list of withheld parts. A Zhihu post linked by one newsletter claims 155 trillion tokens a day per cluster; it is unverified and left out.

Checked 2026-10-26 against the PyTorch blog tables: 98% is 4,821 of 4,917 models; 27.1% MFU is the 8,192-chip weak-scaling row. Secondary coverage quoting "52% MFU on 8,192 chips" misreads the table. Whether Meta's TPUs sit in its own data centres or in Google Cloud is not stated in the primary posts.
The training-side answer to monitors that become targets is [[GRAFT|t-research|i-graft]], and Anthropic's [[UK AISI assessment|t-research|i-aisi]] is the week's incident.
The headline, scores and harnesses are in [[Top stories|t-top|i-kimi]].

Correction 2026-10-26, from the paper page built the same day from the authors' released per-seed data: the blog's rounded figures overstate the penalty and understate GRAFT before ablation. The reward penalty taught undetected hacking on 25.9% of trajectories (not "about 30%"); GRAFT hacked on 38.5% before the adapter was deleted (not "up to 35%") and 1.6% after; the task score was 79.2 against the base model's 60.2 (+19.0, Table 4; Figure 2's metric gives +16.2), while GRAFT's solve rate (74.8%) was slightly below the penalty's (77.2%). The [[animation|t-research|v-graft]] uses the paper's figures.

Correction 2026-10-26, from the paper page built the same day: the 43.6% harness and the "near 36%" student are different tree shapes; the 85-call tree that reaches 43.6% has no student, and the best student of any shape scores 35.8% (at the 7-call tree). The 4B student's 41.6% against its teacher's 40.0% is within half a standard error, so "closed the gap" is right and "passed it" would not be. Adam Block is at Columbia, not CMU.
Follows the ARC-AGI-3 harness gap in {{2026-10-19: tech news|n:3fe5c17b0d0d81828721e0f0f189eb76}}.
